chapterTitle: Integrating NoSQL Databases - MongoDB with PyMongo
aiGenerationNote:
Create a 15-minute mixed-format lesson. Begin with a 3-minute animated comparison of SQL vs. NoSQL (document DBs) using a visual analogy (e.g., rigid spreadsheet vs. flexible folder of diverse forms). Then, transition to a 12-minute live coding demo using PyMongo. Show connecting to a local MongoDB, inserting diverse user documents (emphasizing schema flexibility), and performing `find()`, `find_one()` with various filters and operators (`$gt`, `$lte`, array matching). Demonstrate `update_one()` with `$set` and `$push`, and `delete_one()`. Include clear terminal output showing the MongoDB shell commands for verification. The interactive element should be a drag-and-drop exercise matching MongoDB concepts (document, collection, database) to their relational counterparts.

screens.title: MongoDB & PyMongo: Flexible Data for Python
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will explore why a document database like MongoDB is sometimes a better fit than a rigid S Q L schema, and how PyMongo provides the Pythonic bridge to interact with that data. We begin with a clear definition of document storage and contrast it with relational tables so you appreciate the trade-offs in modeling and scaling. Then we move into hands-on patterns: installing PyMongo, creating a MongoClient, and accessing databases and collections. You will see concrete examples of inserting diverse documents, querying with operators like greater-than and array matching, and modifying documents safely with update operators. Finally, we focus on safety: handling connection errors, avoiding broad delete or update filters, and understanding case sensitivity in queries. By the end of this chapter you should be able to pick when to use MongoDB, connect from Python, perform CRUD patterns, and protect your data from common pitfalls. Think about a real application you maintain — could flexible documents simplify feature changes there?

keyIdea.text: Document databases store JSON-like documents with flexible schemas; PyMongo is the official Python driver that makes CRUD and query operations straightforward while requiring careful error handling and filter checks.

content.html:
Module 09 › Chapter 9.8 › Overview
MongoDB with PyMongo
Integrate flexible document storage into Python applications.

Document databases use JSON-like documents to model data. That means fields can vary across records, enabling rapid iteration and easier horizontal scaling. PyMongo is the official driver that exposes MongoDB concepts in Python.

In this lesson
  • Compare relational vs document models and when to choose each.
  • Install PyMongo and establish connections with MongoClient.
  • Perform safe CRUD operations and apply update operators.
Coming up
A terminal-style hands-on demo will show connecting, inserting diverse user documents, querying with operators, updating with $set and $push, and cautious deletions.
Concept map
Documents → Collections → Databases → PyMongo
Document
A JSON-like record. Example: {'name': 'Alice', 'age': 30, 'interests': ['coding']}.
Collection
A group of documents, similar to a table but schema-free.
Database
A container for collections. Created automatically when you first insert data.
PyMongo
The Python driver. Use MongoClient to connect, then access db.collection.
Explore key topics
Modeling
When to prefer documents over tables for evolving schemas.
CRUD
Insert, query, update, and delete with PyMongo methods.
Safety
Handle connection errors and avoid empty filters that affect all documents.

screens.title: Relational vs Document Databases
screens.narratorSegment: Start by anchoring the main difference: a relational database uses predefined tables with schema constraints and explicit relationships, while a document database stores self-contained, JSON-like documents where each record can have a different shape. This difference matters because it changes how you model change. If your application frequently adds or removes fields, document stores let you iterate quickly without migrations. Conversely, if strict consistency and relational integrity are critical, a S Q L database gives stronger guarantees. A concrete example: a product catalog where every product shares the same columns may fit a table well; but if products across categories carry drastically different attributes, a document per product avoids many nullable columns and migration pain. A common misconception is thinking documents are unstructured; they are semi-structured and can be validated at the application or database level when needed. Another confusion is scaling: relational systems often scale vertically or with careful sharding, while document stores like MongoDB are designed for horizontal partitioning. The key takeaway: choose the model that matches how your data evolves and how you will query it. Which model would reduce friction most for your next feature change?

keyIdea.title: Choose by evolution & access patterns
keyIdea.text: Use relational when schemas and relationships are stable and require strong integrity; choose documents when schema flexibility and horizontal scaling matter.

content.html:
Module 09 › Chapter 9.8 › Relational vs Document
Core claim
Different models, different trade-offs
Relational: fixed schema, joins, ACID guarantees for many transactions.
Document: flexible schema, documents as units, easier horizontal scaling.
Pick a model based on how your data changes and how you query it.
Example
A product catalog with varied attributes per category benefits from documents since each product document can carry only relevant fields.
Common mistake
Treating documents as unstructured blobs. They still deserve thoughtful field design and indexing for queries.
Side-by-side
Relational
  • Predefined schema
  • Normalized tables
  • Stronger transactional guarantees
Document
  • Schema-less documents
  • Denormalized when useful
  • Designed for horizontal scale
Key Takeaway

Model choice should match how your data evolves and how you query it. Flexibility reduces migration cost, but you still need indexes and validation.

screens.title: MongoDB Data Model
screens.narratorSegment: At the heart of MongoDB are documents — self-contained records that look like Python dictionaries with key-value pairs. A single document might include nested objects and arrays, for example a user document with a name, email, list of interests, and a created_at timestamp. Documents are grouped into collections; collections are analogous to tables but do not enforce a single schema. Databases are containers for collections. This layered model changes how you think about relationships: rather than many normalized rows linked by foreign keys, you may embed related data inside a document or reference other documents, depending on access patterns and update frequency. For instance, storing a short list of tags inside a product document makes reads simpler, but if tags change independently or are heavily shared, a reference model could be better. A common misconception is that collections are typed— they are not; you can store different shapes in the same collection. The practical rule: design documents to optimize the queries your application performs most often. How would you model an order that must include line items, shipment details, and a variable list of notes?

content.html:
Module 09 › Chapter 9.8 › Data Model
Term: Document
A JSON-like object, similar to a Python dictionary: keys map to values which can be scalars, arrays, or nested objects.
{ 'name': 'Alice', 'email': 'alice@example.com', 'age': 30, 'interests': ['coding', 'reading'], 'created_at': '2023-09-01T12:00:00' }
When to embed
Embed related data that you read together, like address within a user document.
When to reference
Reference when related data is large or shared across many documents, such as a shared product catalog.
Collections & Databases
Collections group documents. Databases contain collections. Both are created lazily on first insert.
Key Takeaway

Documents are flexible; design them to reflect common access patterns. Collections are organizational, not type-enforced.

Analogy
Think of a collection as a folder of forms; each form can have different fields but serves the same general purpose.

screens.title: Connecting with PyMongo
screens.narratorSegment: Connecting reliably to MongoDB is the first practical step. Use the MongoClient class from PyMongo and supply the connection URI or host and port. A common pattern wraps client creation in a try-except block catching ConnectionFailure and PyMongoError so your application can respond to unreachable hosts or authentication problems gracefully. Once you have a client, access a database attribute and then a collection attribute; these objects are lightweight and do not perform network input and output until you execute an operation. For example, creating client equals MongoClient('mongodb://localhost:27017/') and then db = client. product_catalog and products = db. products. Remember that the database and collection are created on first insert; accessing them does not send commands. A misunderstanding is assuming client creation validates credentials immediately — in many setups validation happens when the first operation runs. Always call client. close() when your work is finished, or use context managers where suitable. Try this pattern in your scripts so connection failures are handled cleanly and resources are closed predictably. Connecting with PyMongo means wrap mongoclient creation in try-except for connectionfailure/pymongoerror and close the client after use to manage resources safely.. In practical terms, establishing mongoclient, accessing databases and collections with error handling. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 09 › Chapter 9.8 › Connecting
Typical connection code
from pymongo import MongoClient
from pymongo.errors import ConnectionFailure, PyMongoError

try:
  client = MongoClient('mongodb://localhost:27017/')
  db = client.product_catalog
  products = db.products
  print('Connected to MongoDB and accessed products collection')
except ConnectionFailure as e:
  print('Could not connect to MongoDB:', e)
  exit()
except PyMongoError as e:
  print('PyMongo error:', e)
  exit()
Note: Database and collection names create resources only on insert. Client creation may be deferred until first operation.
Checklist
  • Install PyMongo with pip before running code.
  • Use try-except for ConnectionFailure and PyMongoError.
  • Close client when done to release resources.
Pro tip
Use a connection URI for cloud instances. Test connectivity with a small read to validate auth credentials.
Key Takeaway

Create MongoClient safely, access db.collection lazily, and always handle connection exceptions to avoid crashes.

screens.title: Inserting Documents with insert_one & insert_many
screens.narratorSegment: Inserting documents is straightforward: pass a Python dictionary to insert_one or a list of dictionaries to insert_many. MongoDB will add an _id field automatically if you do not provide one, returning the new ObjectId via the result object. This is useful for referencing newly created documents. A concrete example: you might insert a user document with name, email, interests, and a created_at timestamp. After inserting, inspect result. inserted_id to capture the id for subsequent operations. A common error is assuming insert_many returns a single id; it returns a list of inserted_ids. Another pitfall is inserting documents with overlapping keys and expecting merge behavior — insert simply creates new documents. When inserting many records in production, consider batching and handling bulk errors. Below is a short code example you can run in your terminal demo. After running an insert, check the collection contents with find({}) to confirm the documents appear as expected. What id will MongoDB assign if you omit the _id field? Inserting Documents with insert_one & insert_many means insert_one returns insertoneresult with inserted_id; insert_many returns insertmanyresult with inserted_ids. mongodb adds _id when missing.. In practical terms, how pymongo creates documents and the automatic _id behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 09 › Chapter 9.8 › Insert Documents
Insert example
# Insert a single document
user_data = {
  'name': 'Alice',
  'email': 'alice@example.com',
  'age': 30,
  'interests': ['coding', 'reading']
}
result_one = users_collection.insert_one(user_data)
print('Inserted one user with ID:', result_one.inserted_id)

# Insert multiple
many_users = [
  {'name': 'Bob', 'email': 'bob@example.com', 'age': 25},
  {'name': 'Charlie', 'email': 'charlie@example.com', 'age': 35}
]
result_many = users_collection.insert_many(many_users)
print('Inserted IDs:', result_many.inserted_ids)
Remember: insert_many returns a list of inserted_ids. Insert operations are immediate writes unless you configure write concern differently.
Example card
Scenario
Add a new user and store the inserted _id so you can link purchases to that user later.
Key Takeaway

Use result.inserted_id(s) to reference newly created documents and avoid assumptions about automatic merging or id formats.

screens.title: Querying Documents with find and find_one
screens.narratorSegment: Reading documents uses find and find_one. find returns a cursor you can iterate; find_one returns a single document or None. Filters are dictionaries: an empty filter returns all documents. Use MongoDB operators like $gt for greater-than and $lte for less-than-or-equal. Array matching is simple — specifying a value for a field containing an array matches documents where the array contains that value. For example, to find users interested in coding, query {'interests': 'coding'}. Combining fields in the same filter performs an implicit logical AND. A frequent misconception is expecting case-insensitive matches by default; queries are case-sensitive unless you use regex or a case-insensitive index. Also avoid holding the entire cursor content in memory for very large collections — iterate or paginate. Below is a concise demo showing find with a filter and printing results. After running a find, consider projecting only the fields you need to reduce bandwidth. How would you find active users older than 25 using a single filter? Querying Documents with find and find_one means find returns a cursor for iteration; filters are dictionaries using mongodb operators; array fields match by element value and queries are case-sensitive by default.. In practical terms, filters, operators, array matching, and cursors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 09 › Chapter 9.8 › Querying
Query examples
# Find all users
for user in users_collection.find({}):
  print(user)

# Users older than 28
for user in users_collection.find({'age': {'$gt': 28}}):
  print(user)

# Users interested in 'coding'
for user in users_collection.find({'interests': 'coding'}):
  print(user)

# Find one by email
alice = users_collection.find_one({'email': 'alice@example.com'})
Consider using projection to return only necessary fields and limit to page results for large datasets.
Notes & pitfalls
  • Queries are case-sensitive unless you use regex or special collation.
  • Combining fields in one filter is an implicit AND.
  • Large result sets should use pagination or projection to reduce memory use.
Key Takeaway

Write precise filters and leverage operators to express conditions; test case sensitivity and use projection to improve efficiency.

screens.title: Modifying Documents with update_one & update_many
screens.narratorSegment: When modifying documents, prefer update operators that change specific fields instead of replacing a whole document unless replacement is intentional. update_one and update_many accept a filter and an update document that uses operators like $set to assign values, $inc to increment numeric fields, and $push to append items to an array. For example, to set Alice's age and status, use $set with the filter matching her name. A common error is calling update without an operator, which replaces the matched document with the provided document and removes other fields unexpectedly. Always inspect result. modified_count to confirm changes. For bulk operations, update_many can set a default status for documents lacking that field by filtering with $exists: False. Another tip: consider using upsert=True when you want to create a document if no match exists, but use it intentionally. After updates, read back the document to verify the precise shape and to avoid surprises from implicit schema assumptions. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 09 › Chapter 9.8 › Updates
Update examples
# Update one: set age and status
update_result = users_collection.update_one(
  {'name': 'Alice'},
  {'$set': {'age': 31, 'status': 'active'}}
)
print('Modified:', update_result.modified_count)

# Update many: add default status
update_many = users_collection.update_many(
  {'status': {'$exists': False}},
  {'$set': {'status': 'pending'}}
)
print('Modified many:', update_many.modified_count)

Pitfall & remedy
Accidental replacement
Providing an update document without operators replaces the matched document. Always use $set or other operators when intending partial updates.
Key Takeaway

Use update operators for granular changes, check modified_count, and test upsert behavior before using in production.

screens.title: Deleting Documents and Safety Checks
screens.narratorSegment: Deleting documents is final and must be done with care. delete_one removes a single matching document, delete_many removes all documents matching a filter. The most dangerous mistake is using an empty filter with delete_many({}), which will remove every document in the collection. Always confirm your filters in a safe environment or with a preliminary find to ensure they target the intended records. For example, test the filter with find before applying delete_many. Also consider soft deletes by setting a flag like deleted: True instead of physically removing records when you may need recovery. Another useful pattern is to log the ids that will be deleted, or run a dry-run that prints matching ids. In production, require confirmation or an approval process for bulk deletions. After deletion, verify the deletion count returned by the result object to ensure your operation had the expected effect. How would you safely remove inactive users that have been inactive for over a year? screens.title: Error Handling and Robust Patterns
screens.narratorSegment: Robust applications handle PyMongo exceptions and confirm operation results. Catch ConnectionFailure to detect that you cannot reach the MongoDB server, and catch the broader PyMongoError for other driver-related issues. When performing operations, inspect result objects: InsertOneResult, InsertManyResult, UpdateResult, and DeleteResult include useful attributes such as inserted_id(s), modified_count, and deleted_count. Use these to programmatically confirm success and perform retries or compensating actions if needed. Always close the client connection when work is complete; failing to close can leak resources. Another pattern is to guard dangerous operations behind checks: preview matching ids, require administrative approval for bulk deletes, and avoid blind update_many with empty filters. A common misconception is that PyMongo silently retries on its own. In many cases you must implement retries with backoff for transient network errors. Typical try-except
from pymongo.errors import ConnectionFailure, PyMongoError

  client = MongoClient('mongodb://localhost:27017/')

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Misconceptions
screens.narratorSegment: A quick tour of frequent mistakes will save time. First, remember that MongoDB queries are case-sensitive by default. If you search for a name with different capitalization, you may get no results unless you use regex or a case-insensitive collation. Second, updates without operators replace whole documents; to change a single field use $set, or you risk losing other fields. Third, delete_many with an empty filter will remove all documents in a collection — always preview with find first. Fourth, assume MongoClient will always validate credentials on creation; some connection modes verify only when the first operation triggers network activity. Fifth, treat bulk inserts and updates with care: they may raise bulk write errors that you must catch. Finally, avoid assuming collections enforce a type; they are schema-flexible. The practical remedy is to write small, testable scripts that preview filters, log operation results, and catch PyMongo exceptions. What checks will you add to your next database script to catch these mistakes early? fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will explore why a document database like MongoDB is sometimes a better fit than a rigid S Q L schema, and how PyMongo provides the Pythonic bridge to interact with that data. We begin with a clear definition of document storage and contrast it with relational tables so you appreciate the trade-offs in modeling and scaling. Then we move into hands-on patterns: installing PyMongo, creating a MongoClient, and accessing databases and collections. You will see concrete examples of inserting diverse documents, querying with operators like greater-than and array matching, and modifying documents safely with update operators. Finally, we focus on safety: handling connection errors, avoiding broad delete or update filters, and understanding case sensitivity in queries. By the end of this chapter you should be able to pick when to use MongoDB, connect from Python, perform CRUD patterns, and protect your data from common pitfalls. Think about a real application you maintain — could flexible documents simplify feature changes there?

Over these two screens we will break the chapter goals into practical, verifiable skills. First, you will learn to explain the core differences between relational and NoSQL document databases: how schemas, relationships, and scaling trade-offs shape your design choices. Understanding that distinction helps you choose the right tool for an evolving dataset. Second, you will master MongoDB’s basic vocabulary — what documents, collections, and databases are — and how they map to Python structures. Third, you will install PyMongo and make a robust connection to a running MongoDB instance. Fourth, you will practice creating documents and collections so you can model example data like user profiles without defining a schema first. Each objective is framed so you can demonstrate competency by running the starter code and answering short verification prompts. The next screen continues with CRUD operations and error handling milestones.

This second objectives screen focuses on practical operations and protecting your data. You will learn to perform read queries using find and find_one with filters and operators like greater-than and array membership. That means writing queries that return all documents, one document, or a filtered subset. You will practice update patterns using update_one and update_many together with operators such as $set and $push so you can change specific fields without overwriting other data. We will show delete_one and delete_many while emphasizing the danger of empty filters. Finally, you will implement error handling with ConnectionFailure and PyMongoError so your application can fail gracefully and close connections reliably. These skills let you safely integrate MongoDB into production Python code. Learning Objectives — Practical Skills means master querying, targeted updates, cautious deletions, and error handling to build dependable mongodb integrations.. In practical terms, hands-on operations and robustness targets. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Start by anchoring the main difference: a relational database uses predefined tables with schema constraints and explicit relationships, while a document database stores self-contained, JSON-like documents where each record can have a different shape. This difference matters because it changes how you model change. If your application frequently adds or removes fields, document stores let you iterate quickly without migrations. Conversely, if strict consistency and relational integrity are critical, a S Q L database gives stronger guarantees. A concrete example: a product catalog where every product shares the same columns may fit a table well; but if products across categories carry drastically different attributes, a document per product avoids many nullable columns and migration pain. A common misconception is thinking documents are unstructured; they are semi-structured and can be validated at the application or database level when needed. Another confusion is scaling: relational systems often scale vertically or with careful sharding, while document stores like MongoDB are designed for horizontal partitioning. The key takeaway: choose the model that matches how your data evolves and how you will query it. Which model would reduce friction most for your next feature change?

At the heart of MongoDB are documents — self-contained records that look like Python dictionaries with key-value pairs. A single document might include nested objects and arrays, for example a user document with a name, email, list of interests, and a created_at timestamp. Documents are grouped into collections; collections are analogous to tables but do not enforce a single schema. Databases are containers for collections. This layered model changes how you think about relationships: rather than many normalized rows linked by foreign keys, you may embed related data inside a document or reference other documents, depending on access patterns and update frequency. For instance, storing a short list of tags inside a product document makes reads simpler, but if tags change independently or are heavily shared, a reference model could be better. A common misconception is that collections are typed— they are not; you can store different shapes in the same collection. The practical rule: design documents to optimize the queries your application performs most often. How would you model an order that must include line items, shipment details, and a variable list of notes?

Connecting reliably to MongoDB is the first practical step. Use the MongoClient class from PyMongo and supply the connection URI or host and port. A common pattern wraps client creation in a try-except block catching ConnectionFailure and PyMongoError so your application can respond to unreachable hosts or authentication problems gracefully. Once you have a client, access a database attribute and then a collection attribute; these objects are lightweight and do not perform network input and output until you execute an operation. For example, creating client equals MongoClient('mongodb://localhost:27017/') and then db = client. product_catalog and products = db. products. Remember that the database and collection are created on first insert; accessing them does not send commands. A misunderstanding is assuming client creation validates credentials immediately — in many setups validation happens when the first operation runs. Always call client. close() when your work is finished, or use context managers where suitable. Try this pattern in your scripts so connection failures are handled cleanly and resources are closed predictably. Connecting with PyMongo means wrap mongoclient creation in try-except for connectionfailure/pymongoerror and close the client after use to manage resources safely.. In practical terms, establishing mongoclient, accessing databases and collections with error handling. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Inserting documents is straightforward: pass a Python dictionary to insert_one or a list of dictionaries to insert_many. MongoDB will add an _id field automatically if you do not provide one, returning the new ObjectId via the result object. This is useful for referencing newly created documents. A concrete example: you might insert a user document with name, email, interests, and a created_at timestamp. After inserting, inspect result. inserted_id to capture the id for subsequent operations. A common error is assuming insert_many returns a single id; it returns a list of inserted_ids. Another pitfall is inserting documents with overlapping keys and expecting merge behavior — insert simply creates new documents. When inserting many records in production, consider batching and handling bulk errors. Below is a short code example you can run in your terminal demo. After running an insert, check the collection contents with find({}) to confirm the documents appear as expected. What id will MongoDB assign if you omit the _id field? Inserting Documents with insert_one & insert_many means insert_one returns insertoneresult with inserted_id; insert_many returns insertmanyresult with inserted_ids. mongodb adds _id when missing.. In practical terms, how pymongo creates documents and the automatic _id behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Reading documents uses find and find_one. find returns a cursor you can iterate; find_one returns a single document or None. Filters are dictionaries: an empty filter returns all documents. Use MongoDB operators like $gt for greater-than and $lte for less-than-or-equal. Array matching is simple — specifying a value for a field containing an array matches documents where the array contains that value. For example, to find users interested in coding, query {'interests': 'coding'}. Combining fields in the same filter performs an implicit logical AND. A frequent misconception is expecting case-insensitive matches by default; queries are case-sensitive unless you use regex or a case-insensitive index. Also avoid holding the entire cursor content in memory for very large collections — iterate or paginate. Below is a concise demo showing find with a filter and printing results. After running a find, consider projecting only the fields you need to reduce bandwidth. How would you find active users older than 25 using a single filter? Querying Documents with find and find_one means find returns a cursor for iteration; filters are dictionaries using mongodb operators; array fields match by element value and queries are case-sensitive by default.. In practical terms, filters, operators, array matching, and cursors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

When modifying documents, prefer update operators that change specific fields instead of replacing a whole document unless replacement is intentional. update_one and update_many accept a filter and an update document that uses operators like $set to assign values, $inc to increment numeric fields, and $push to append items to an array. For example, to set Alice's age and status, use $set with the filter matching her name. A common error is calling update without an operator, which replaces the matched document with the provided document and removes other fields unexpectedly. A quick tour of frequent mistakes will save time. First, remember that MongoDB queries are case-sensitive by default. If you search for a name with different capitalization, you may get no results unless you use regex or a case-insensitive collation. Second, updates without operators replace whole documents; to change a single field use $set, or you risk losing other fields. Third, delete_many with an empty filter will remove all documents in a collection — always preview with find first. Fourth, assume MongoClient will always validate credentials on creation; some connection modes verify only when the first operation triggers network activity. Fifth, treat bulk inserts and updates with care: they may raise bulk write errors that you must catch. Finally, avoid assuming collections enforce a type; they are schema-flexible.
